author: kevaundray
content:

I think outside of PQ, the main reason to do 8298 is that it allows one to permanently retire the EOA "master key"; though I haven't checked how much of an issue this is in practice

author: kevaundray
content: What would you be looking for re frames adding PQ support? (I'm just thinking that maybe in all approaches, we will likely need to upgrade the EOA)

author: daniellehrner
content:
I think the main issue is that SETCODEFROM is irreversible. An attacker tricking a user into setting a malicious contract means the user has lost all their funds without any way to fix that. It does make sense as a cheap way to create clones or proxies though.

EIP-7851 would have made more sense for retiring the ECDSA, but we also only had it in C tier in the Hegota ranking and it was already DFI'd

author: draganrakita
content: Solution needs to be irreversible, as we need to block ecdsa signatures from making changes to account. But seeing first how pq sigs is going to work in parallel with ecdsa and then thinking how to nuke them is imo better flow.

author: kevaundray
content: Right, my understanding is that we could have done 7851 + 8151 or 8298 + 8151 as an overall solution

author: ben_a_adams
content: Yes, but you have to do 7702 to get to a contract with SETCODEFROM so is two step and not an accidental call (as you have to in the contract) i.e. you have to sign twice

author: ben_a_adams
content:
We pretend code is completely immutable but then can proxy; so is mutable just with extra steps, extra contract loads and harder to see.

If a contract contains SETCODEFROM opcode you immediately know its mutable with a simple scan

author: ben_a_adams
content:
This one is more urgent due to its other uses and that we are pushing up contract costs deployment costs both with 8037 and increasing calldata costs

So if contracts are duplicates (with 99% are); you only pay for a codehash change rather than having to pay for all the code; and client having to do additional work making and hashing it

Like if Uniswap v2/v3 deploys a new liquidity pool then you pay for all the code, hashing etc; but its really just a hash change
